**XCTest, step by step.** An `XCTestCase` usually has a property holding the object being tested (the "sut", short for *system under test*). The instance method `setUp()` runs before EACH test method and builds that object from scratch, so one test never inherits leftovers from another. There is also `tearDown()` (after each test) and the `setUpWithError() throws` variants. By contrast, `class func setUp()` runs only once for the whole class.
`final class CalculadoraTests: XCTestCase {`
`    var sut: Calculadora!`
`    override func setUp() { sut = Calculadora() }`
`    func testSoma() { XCTAssertEqual(sut.soma(2, 3), 5) }`
`}`

Other assertions the questions use: `XCTAssertNil(x)` passes if `x` is `nil` (its pair is `XCTAssertNotNil`). `XCTAssertThrowsError(try validar(-1))` passes only if the expression throws; a second closure lets you inspect the error received. For `Double`, never compare with exact equality, because `0.1 + 0.2` is not exactly `0.3`: use `XCTAssertEqual(a, b, accuracy: 0.0001)`.

**Callback code and performance.** For a completion handler, create `let e = expectation(description: "done")`, call `e.fulfill()` inside the callback and wait with `await fulfillment(of: [e], timeout: 1)` (or `wait(for:timeout:)`): the test waits only as long as needed, with no `sleep`. The `measure { ... }` block runs the code several times and compares the time with a baseline to detect slowdowns. Code coverage (Edit Scheme > Test > Code Coverage) only tells which lines were executed, not whether the assertions are any good. For UI tests, `XCUIApplication().launch()` opens the app and `app.buttons["Entrar"].tap()` simulates taps.

**Swift Testing in detail.** The `#expect(condition)` macro checks a condition and shows the values involved when it fails. To check that code throws an error: `#expect(throws: ErroIdade.self) { try validar(-1) }` (the label is `throws:` and it takes the error's TYPE). The `#require` macro is the version that stops the test: `let u = try #require(buscar())` unwraps the optional and, if it is `nil`, ends the test right away (that is why it takes `try`).

Parameterized tests run the same function with several inputs, and each input is reported separately: `@Test(arguments: [2, 4, 6]) func ePar(n: Int) { #expect(n % 2 == 0) }`. To group tests across files, declare a tag and use it as a trait: `extension Tag { @Tag static var rede: Self }` and `@Test(.tags(.rede)) func baixa() async { }`; now you can filter, for example, only the network tests. A type that contains `@Test` functions (with an optional `@Suite`) forms a suite, and each test runs on a fresh instance of it.

**Rule of thumb (F.I.R.S.T.):** good tests are Fast, Independent (never depend on execution order, which can vary and is parallel in Swift Testing), Repeatable (same result every time), Self-validating (they pass or fail on their own) and Timely (written at the right moment).

**Sending data with POST.** To create a resource on the server, build a `URLRequest`, change the method and put the JSON in the body:
`var req = URLRequest(url: url)`
`req.httpMethod = "POST"`
`req.setValue("application/json", forHTTPHeaderField: "Content-Type")`
`req.httpBody = try JSONEncoder().encode(usuario)`
`let (data, response) = try await URLSession.shared.data(for: req)`
`Content-Type` is the HTTP header that describes the media type of the body; without it the server may not realize the body is JSON. `encode` is the opposite of `decode`: it turns the `Codable` value into `Data`.

**snake_case keys.** Many APIs use `nome_completo` (snake_case), while Swift uses `nomeCompleto` (camelCase). Instead of writing `CodingKeys`, you can set `decoder.keyDecodingStrategy = .convertFromSnakeCase`. It works when the convention is consistent; if a name breaks the rule, go back to `CodingKeys`. ISO 8601 dates follow the same idea with `decoder.dateDecodingStrategy = .iso8601`.

**Decoding errors.** `DecodingError` has these cases: `keyNotFound` (a required key is missing), `typeMismatch` (different type: `"5"` where an `Int` was expected; `JSONDecoder` does not convert on its own), `valueNotFound` (a `null` came where a value was expected) and `dataCorrupted` (malformed JSON). To filter: `catch let e as DecodingError { ... }`. When the JSON looks very different from the model (nested, alternative values), write `init(from decoder: Decoder) throws` and use `decoder.container(keyedBy:)` to decode field by field. To be `Codable`, all stored properties must also be `Codable` (basic types, arrays, dictionaries and optionals already are).

**Sessions, timeout and download.** `URLSession.shared` uses the default configuration. `URLSessionConfiguration.ephemeral` creates a "private" session: cache, cookies and credentials stay only in memory. The default `timeoutInterval` of a `URLRequest` is 60 seconds; when it runs out, `URLError.timedOut` is thrown. For large files, `URLSession.shared.download(from: url)` writes to a temporary file instead of loading everything into memory (to continue in the background, use a `.background` session). If the `Task` that called `data(from:)` is cancelled, the request is cancelled and throws a `URLError` with code `.cancelled`, which is usually handled silently.

**HTTPS, secrets and tests.** App Transport Security (ATS) requires HTTPS by default; plain HTTP needs an exception in Info.plist (avoid `NSAllowsArbitraryLoads`). Login tokens go in the Keychain, never in the source code or in `UserDefaults`. To test without calling the real server, hide the network behind a protocol (`protocol Servico { func buscar() async throws -> [Usuario] }`) and inject a fake version in tests; a custom `URLProtocol` that returns fixed responses also works.

**Everyday tools.** The `ModelContext` comes from the environment: `@Environment(\.modelContext) private var contexto`. The key is the type name with a lowercase first letter. To guarantee a unique value per record (an e-mail, for example), use `@Attribute(.unique) var email: String`; when you insert a duplicate, SwiftData updates the existing record. `@Transient` marks a property that must NOT be persisted (temporary or UI values). To build a form that edits a `@Model`, use `@Bindable var tarefa: Tarefa` and then `TextField("Title", text: $tarefa.titulo)`. A `@Model` is already observable (it includes the Observation framework), which is why the View updates without `@Published`.

**Sorting and filtering in `@Query`.** `@Query(sort: \Tarefa.criada, order: .reverse) var tarefas: [Tarefa]` sorts from largest to smallest (newest to oldest); `.forward` is the default (ascending). Filters: `@Query(filter: #Predicate<Tarefa> { !$0.feita })` brings only the pending ones (`!$0.feita` is true when `feita` is `false`). Unlike the `filter` of an array, `#Predicate` is translated into a query on the store, without loading everything into memory.

**Why `@Query` and not `fetch` + `@State`?** If you fetch with `try context.fetch(...)` in `onAppear` and keep the result in `@State`, you hold a copy that becomes stale when something is inserted or deleted. `@Query` rebuilds the list by itself. Outside Views (in a service, for example), use `FetchDescriptor`, which gathers `predicate`, `sortBy` and `fetchLimit`:
`var d = FetchDescriptor<Tarefa>(predicate: #Predicate { !$0.feita })`
`d.fetchLimit = 20`
`let lote = try contexto.fetch(d)`
To delete in bulk: `try contexto.delete(model: Tarefa.self, where: #Predicate { $0.feita })`.

**Saving, in-memory storage and relationships.** Normally you do NOT need to call `context.save()` after each `insert`: the main context has autosave. A manual save exists for specific cases (before a critical operation). For previews and tests, use memory-only storage: `.modelContainer(for: Tarefa.self, inMemory: true)` on the scene/View, or manually `ModelContainer(for: Tarefa.self, configurations: ModelConfiguration(isStoredInMemoryOnly: true))`. In `@Relationship(deleteRule:)`, `.nullify` (the default) keeps the children and sets the reference to `nil`; `.cascade` deletes the children too; `.deny` prevents deleting the parent while children exist.

**Migration and iCloud.** If the schema changes between app versions (renaming a property, for example), describe the versions with `VersionedSchema` and the steps with `SchemaMigrationPlan`, to transform existing data without loss. To sync with iCloud (CloudKit), the model must respect restrictions: no `.unique`, properties optional or with a default value, and optional relationships.

**Several `catch` blocks, in order.** `catch` blocks are tested from top to bottom and the first one that matches wins; a final `catch` with no pattern catches the rest. You can match specific cases, extract associated values and filter by type:
`do { try sacar(500) }`
`catch ErroSaque.semSaldo(let faltam) { print("Missing \(faltam)") }`
`catch let e as DecodingError { print(e) }`
`catch { print(error.localizedDescription) }`
If `f()` throws `Erro.b` and there is only `catch Erro.a` plus a generic `catch`, the generic one runs.

**The `try` rule.** A function NOT marked `throws` cannot let an error escape. So `try f()` inside it only compiles if it is in a `do/catch` that handles all errors (with a generic `catch`) or if you use `try?`/`try!`. To give a `try?` a default value: `let n = (try? f()) ?? 0` (remember that `try?` discards the cause of the error). In asynchronous functions, the order is `func f() async throws` and the call is `try await f()`.

**`defer` runs in reverse order.** Several `defer` blocks in the same scope run like a stack (LIFO): the last one declared runs first. With `defer { print(1) }` followed by `defer { print(2) }`, the output is 2 and then 1. This lets you undo actions in the right order.

**Friendly messages.** `error.localizedDescription` returns a generic text for any error. To control the text, make the type adopt `LocalizedError` and implement `errorDescription`:
`enum ErroSaque: LocalizedError { case semSaldo`
`    var errorDescription: String? { "Insufficient balance" } }`

**`Result` and initializers.** `Result { try f() }` runs the closure and returns `.success(value)` or `.failure(error)`. An `init?` returns `nil` without saying why; an `init() throws` throws an error with the cause: prefer the latter when the caller needs to know why it failed.

**Programmer failures: `assert`, `precondition`, `fatalError`.** Expected errors (network, validation, wrong password) use `throws`. A state that should never happen, on the other hand, is a programmer bug, and then the program stops: `assert(x >= 0)` is only checked in debug builds; `precondition(x >= 0)` also in release; `fatalError("impossible")` always ends the app. Do not use these functions for errors the user can cause.

**Small details of the game code.** `tentativas += 1` is compound assignment: it reads the value, adds 1 and writes it back (equivalent to `tentativas = tentativas + 1`). Inside the "Novo jogo" button, you draw another secret by assigning to the state variable that holds it: `alvo = Int.random(in: 1...100)`.

**Modifiers and layout parameters.** `.disabled(condition)` blocks taps on a control while the condition is `true`: `Button("Chutar") { verificar() }.disabled(Int(palpite) == nil)` keeps the button inactive until the text is a valid number. In a `VStack(spacing: 16) { ... }`, the `spacing` parameter sets the distance between children. To limit the input up front, controls such as `Stepper(value: $n, in: 1...100)` already prevent invalid entries by construction.

**Why can `@State` change inside a method without `mutating`?** A struct normally requires `mutating` to change its properties. But `@State` does not keep the value inside the struct: the value lives in storage managed by SwiftUI, and the struct only holds a wrapper pointing to it. Since the wrapper's setter is not `mutating`, `verificar()` can change the state. The `$` prefix accesses the `projectedValue` of `@State`, a `Binding<String>` (read and write); `palpite` without `$` is just the `String`.

**Ranges and conversion.** `1...100` is a CLOSED range (includes 100); `1..<100` is half-open (goes up to 99). `Int(" 42")` returns `nil`, because spaces invalidate the conversion; use `trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespaces)` first. String interpolation `"Acertou em \(tentativas)!"` inserts the value into the string. In binary search (always guess the middle), each guess eliminates half of the options; since 2^7 = 128 ≥ 100, 7 attempts are enough.

**Challenge extras.** `@FocusState private var focado: Bool` with `.focused($focado)` on the `TextField` lets you dismiss the keyboard by setting `focado = false`. `@AppStorage("recorde") var recorde = 0` stores a simple value in `UserDefaults` and survives restarts (`@State` lives only while the View exists). An alert uses a state Bool: `.alert("Congratulations", isPresented: $venceu) { Button("OK") { } }`. The business rule (such as the attempt limit) lives in `verificar()`; the interface just reflects the state.

**One binding per element.** `ForEach($tarefas) { $t in ... }` (note the `$` before the array and the `$t` in the closure) hands you a `Binding` for EACH element, so you can edit directly: `ForEach($tarefas) { $t in Toggle(t.titulo, isOn: $t.feita) }`. Without the `$`, `t` is just a read-only copy.

**Identity and `Identifiable`.** `ForEach(tarefas)` works without `id:` because `Tarefa` adopts `Identifiable` and `ForEach` uses the `id` property. The `id` must be stable: if you create `Tarefa(...)` inside the View body, every update generates a new `UUID` and SwiftUI treats the rows as brand-new items (losing state and animations). Watch out with `Codable`: in `struct Tarefa: Codable { let id = UUID(); var titulo: String }`, a `let` with an initial value is NOT decoded (the compiler warns); use `var id = UUID()` or `let id: UUID` so the id is persisted.

**Useful `String` and `Array` members.** `novoTitulo.isEmpty` is `true` when there are no characters: `guard !novoTitulo.isEmpty else { return }` (to ignore whitespace-only input, first use `trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespaces)`). `tarefas.removeAll(where: { $0.feita })` removes every element that satisfies the condition. `tarefas.filter { !$0.feita }.count` counts the pending ones (3 tasks, 2 done, gives 1).

**Navigation, empty state and editing.** `NavigationStack { ... }` is the navigation container (it replaces the old `NavigationView`); `.navigationTitle("Tarefas")` only tells the container's bar the title, so without a `NavigationStack` nothing displays it. For an empty list: `ContentUnavailableView("No tasks", systemImage: "checklist")`. `List` reuses rows and brings swipe and editing for free; a `VStack` does not. For custom swipe actions (archive, mark), use `.swipeActions(edge:)`; `.onDelete` is just the shortcut for removing. To reorder, `.onMove { tarefas.move(fromOffsets: $0, toOffset: $1) }` (with an `EditButton`). `.onSubmit { adicionar() }` on a `TextField` runs when Return is pressed.

**Pitfalls.** In a filtered list, the `onDelete` offsets refer to the FILTERED list; applying them to the full array deletes the wrong tasks, so map to the ids and remove by id. `@AppStorage` supports simple types (Bool, Int, String, Data...), not a `[Tarefa]` directly: encode with `Codable` or use SwiftData. To share the list across screens (iOS 17+), use an `@Observable` class kept in `@State` at the root and passed down.

**Usability tests and research questions.** A usability test means watching real people use the prototype, without helping them, to see where they get stuck; the people who built the app know it too well to notice these problems. When interviewing, ask open, neutral questions ("Tell me how you organize your tasks today") and avoid questions that lead the answer ("Don't you think the app is amazing?").

**Prototype before coding.** Paper or a drawing tool (such as Figma) lets you change an idea in minutes; rewriting code costs far more. The earlier a design mistake shows up, the cheaper it is to fix. A static wireframe shows the structure; an interactive prototype links the screens, so you can tap and navigate to evaluate the flow.

**The cycle continues after launch.** If the test shows that nobody finds the "Save" button, the answer is to iterate: adjust the button, create a new version and test again (neither ignoring the problem nor redoing the whole app). After launch, reviews, metrics and new iOS versions reopen the cycle, and planning includes defining the audience, goals, features, priorities and what goes into the MVP.

**SwiftUI in practice.** A semantic text style is applied with `.font(...)`: `Text("Resumo").font(.headline)`. `.headline` is an emphasized style (bold by default) that scales with Dynamic Type, unlike `.font(.system(size: 12))`, which is fixed. For an icon, `Image(systemName: "star.fill")` loads an SF Symbol (whereas `Image("name")` loads an image from your asset catalog). For a background that fills the whole screen, including behind the safe areas: `Color.blue.ignoresSafeArea()`.

**Tabs and modals.** Each tab of a `TabView` is a View marked with `.tabItem`, which sets the icon and title:
`TabView {`
`    Text("Início").tabItem { Label("Início", systemImage: "house") }`
`}`
A `sheet` presents modal content (`.sheet(isPresented: $mostra) { ... }`), suited to a focused, independent task such as creating a new item; drilling into details uses a push on the `NavigationStack`, and the main sections use the tab bar.

**Feedback and adaptation.** `.sensoryFeedback(.success, trigger: salvou)` fires a success haptic every time the value of `salvou` changes (for example, `salvou.toggle()` in the button). Haptics reinforce visual feedback; they do not replace it. For screens of different sizes (iPhone SE to Pro Max), prefer adaptive layouts with stacks and `Spacer` instead of fixed positions. Colors and images in the asset catalog accept Light/Dark variants, and you should test both modes in Previews. A small button can keep a small icon and enlarge the tappable area up to 44 x 44 points (points are resolution-independent units, not pixels).

**Combining elements and describing images.** A list row with an icon and a title would be read by VoiceOver as two elements. To merge them into one: `HStack { Image(systemName: "star"); Text("Favoritos") }.accessibilityElement(children: .combine)`. For meaningful images, the text should be short and significant ("Ana's profile photo"); file names ("IMG_2048.png") and generic terms ("image", "click here") do not help. Decorative images get `.accessibilityHidden(true)`.

**Contrast and color.** The guidelines (WCAG) ask for a contrast of at least 4.5:1 between text and background for normal text; light gray on white usually fails. The Accessibility Inspector measures contrast and also lists labels, traits and small touch targets. Never rely on color alone: a "No connection" indicator that is just a red circle is not noticed by people with color blindness; combine it with text, an icon or a shape.

**Large text and Reduce Motion.** With Dynamic Type, use semantic styles (`.font(.body)`) and layouts that grow and allow several lines; do not use fixed sizes or cut everything to one line with "...". For Reduce Motion, read `@Environment(\.accessibilityReduceMotion) var reduzir` and replace intense animations (parallax, zoom) with simple fades when `reduzir` is `true`.

**RTL languages and localization.** In right-to-left languages (Arabic, Hebrew), SwiftUI mirrors the layout automatically, as long as you use `leading` and `trailing` edges (for example, `.padding(.leading, 8)`) instead of fixed left and right. Localizing an app involves text, dates, numbers, currencies and text direction; in Xcode, translations live in String Catalogs.

**Really testing it.** SwiftUI helps, but useful labels and a logical flow depend on you: use the app with VoiceOver, large text and Reduce Motion turned on, and test with real people. Inclusive design means thinking from the start about diversity of abilities, languages and contexts, rather than adding accessibility after launch.

**Permissions and Info.plist.** Each sensitive resource has its usage-description key, and the text appears in the permission alert, so it must be honest and specific (for example, "We use your location to show nearby stores"). If the app accesses the resource WITHOUT the key, iOS terminates the app (crash). For tracking across apps and other companies' sites, besides the request via `ATTrackingManager.requestTrackingAuthorization { status in ... }`, you need the `NSUserTrackingUsageDescription` key; apps that do not track do not need the alert. Ask for permission at the moment the user uses the feature that needs it, explaining why, and if they deny it the app should keep working in a limited way.

**Data in transit and at rest.** Encryption turns data into a format unreadable to anyone without the key; it protects data in transit (HTTPS, which uses TLS) and at rest (storage). Compressing a file is NOT encrypting it. ATS requires HTTPS by default: allowing HTTP across the whole app leaves traffic readable to anyone on the same network, so prefer HTTPS and, if unavoidable, per-domain exceptions. Passwords and tokens go in the Keychain: `UserDefaults` writes to a readable file inside the app and can expose the value in backups or jailbroken devices.

**Transparency and laws.** The App Store privacy nutrition labels show, before download, which data the app collects and how it is used (stating it wrongly violates store rules). The privacy manifest is the `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy` file (extension `.xcprivacy`). Data minimization means collecting only what is necessary (asking only for the e-mail, not the ID number and address), which reduces risk in leaks. LGPD (Brazil), GDPR (Europe) and COPPA (USA, protects children under 13) are laws that regulate the collection and processing of personal data. Phishing is the social engineering that tricks a person with fake messages or sites; urgency and a request for a password through a link are classic signs.

**Social impact.** The digital divide is the inequality of access to devices, internet and digital skills: think of slow connections and old devices. Algorithmic bias happens when a model trained on biased historical data reproduces and amplifies inequalities (for example, recommending jobs only to men); the answer is to audit the data, test with diverse groups and allow appeals. Infinite scroll and constant notifications designed to hold attention can cause compulsive use; break reminders and time limits help.
